title: Is It in Stock? Inventory, Availability and the Promise You Can Keep
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/10-inventory-and-availability/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter. It is a contract, not a description: the places where the chapter did not yet do what the spec asks are listed under open_questions.

know: The five stock numbers (on hand, committed, reserved, held back, incoming) and the available-to-promise figure derived from them.
The three moments at which a unit can become promised (cart, order, fulfillment) and what each costs.
The parts of an availability service and which system writes which number.
believe: 'Available' is a computation that no system should store as a fact and let another overwrite.
Oversells come from several writers and from scheduled copying, not from a system that cannot count.
can_do: Compute available-to-promise from on hand, committed, reserved and held-back units.
Name, for their own company, the system of record for on hand at each location and the only writer of committed.
Say when a merchant needs a separate availability service.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the integration or back-end engineer who inherits a stock synchronization and needs to know which system should own which number before touching it. Operations and e-commerce managers get the vocabulary for a conversation about buffers and oversells.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side.
Roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
Kestrel & Pine, its people, its 2026 incidents in outline and the names of the failure patterns (meet-kestrel-and-pine, where-commerce-platforms-go-wrong).

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, the business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, and the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From the earlier chapters of Part II: who owns product content, prices and discounts, and that the search index is a copy that showed the Ridgewalker 'in stock' from a stock figure up to two hours old.
does_not_know: The stock numbers: on hand, committed (allocated), reserved, held back, safety stock, incoming, and available-to-promise (ATP).
Reserve-on-cart, reserve-on-order and allocation at fulfillment; the consistency window.
Location, per-channel buffer, sourcing, allocation for a customer, backorder, pre-order, inventory valuation.
Stock event, snapshot against change, synchronous call, atomic commit, eventual consistency in plain words.
Cycle counting and inventory record inaccuracy.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given the stock numbers for one product at one location, the reader computes what a channel may still sell and names the result as derived.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A warehouse has 10 jackets on the shelf. 3 belong to placed orders that have not shipped, 1 is reserved in a cart, and 2 are held back as a buffer. Using only this chapter: how many may a channel still sell, and what is that number called?
acceptance_criteria.expected: 4: on hand minus committed minus reserved minus held back. It is available-to-promise (or 'available'), a derived number, not a count.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two channels that sold the same last unit, the reader names several writers and scheduled copying as causes and does not accept a shorter sync interval as the whole remedy.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Two channels sold the same last unit. Using only this chapter: which causes would you look for, and would copying stock every five minutes instead of every hour fix it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Several systems writing the same stock number; copying on a schedule, so each channel learns of the other's sales late; a reservation window; a wrong count; no buffer. A shorter interval shortens the lag and leaves the writers. The remedy is one writer for on hand and one for committed, stock changes sent as events, 'available' computed in one place per channel with a buffer, and a reconciliation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say which interaction must get an exact answer from the availability service and which may read a slightly stale copy.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: which step of a purchase must ask the availability service and wait for the answer, and which steps may show a slightly old figure?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Checkout, at order creation: the unit is committed atomically so the last unit goes to exactly one order. The 'in stock' badge on listing pages, add to cart and the marketplace stock push may read a slightly stale copy.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: What 'in stock' means as several numbers; when a unit becomes promised; many locations and channels; the availability service and what each interaction needs; events against scheduled copying; the choices and their trade-offs by scale stage; Kestrel & Pine's Oversell worked through; how stock integrations fail. Evidence: the Black Friday Oversell, platform documentation, a study of inventory record accuracy.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].
A reader new to commerce meets no term in this chapter before it is explained, and every acronym is expanded on first use.

thesis.question: What does "in stock" mean, who computes it, and how do you avoid selling what you do not have?
thesis.claim: 'In stock' means available-to-promise: units on hand minus three amounts: units committed to orders, units held temporarily for carts, and units held back as a buffer. This figure is computed in one place and published to each channel: by the shop platform while the shop platform is the only system that takes orders and counts stock, and, once a second system takes orders or counts stock, by one service that receives every count and every commitment. A merchant avoids selling what it does not have by giving on hand and committed one writer each, sending each stock change as an event when it happens instead of copying totals on a schedule, holding back a buffer per channel, and committing a unit to exactly one order at checkout.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that stock is one number which each system holds and synchronizes with the others, so that an oversell is cured by synchronizing more often.
thesis.so_what: On Black Friday 2026 Kestrel & Pine oversold 1,340 units on 1,120 orders, at a cost of about €96,000, while every system was up and reporting its own number. A merchant that accepts the claim writes down who owns each stock number before it builds the first connector.
thesis.how_why: A stored 'available' figure can be overwritten by any system that copies it, so two writers, or one copy made on a schedule, leave channels selling from different answers; at Kestrel & Pine's peak of 38 orders a minute, a one-hour copy interval can hide up to about 2,300 orders from the other channels. Deriving the figure in one place, from one counted fact and one list of commitments, leaves one answer for every channel, and only the commit at checkout has to be exact.

supporting_claims.claim: 'In stock' is a derived figure, available-to-promise: on hand, the one counted fact, minus the units committed to orders, reserved for carts and held back on purpose; a system that stores it as a fact and lets another system overwrite it has prepared an oversell.

The moment a unit becomes promised (cart, order or fulfillment) is a business choice with a cost on each side, and only the commit at checkout has to be exact: there the last unit must go to exactly one order.

The figure is computed in one place and published per channel: by the shop platform while it is the only system that takes orders and counts stock, and by one availability service, with a buffer per channel, once a second system takes orders or counts stock.

Oversells come from several writers of one number and from totals copied on a schedule, so the remedy is one writer each for on hand and committed and stock changes sent as events when they happen, not a shorter copying interval.

The counted fact is itself often wrong and events are sometimes lost or repeated, so the design is finished only with a deliberate buffer and a scheduled comparison of every copy with the system that counts.

role.contribution: Applies the part's argument to the fastest-changing fact, where a stale copy costs most, and performs the part's closing before handing the committed unit to the cart.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene then five-numbers to service: the Oversell, then the terms and the arrangement that answer it
choices, trade-offs and stages: four options on the same criteria, then by stage

flow.rationale: The Oversell comes first so that every term arrives as part of the answer to 'why did the website not know'. The five numbers follow because nothing can be said about ownership until the reader knows which number is counted and which is derived; the moment of promise follows the numbers because it is the moment a unit moves from one of them to another. Locations and channels come after both: 'available per channel' needs 'available', and the wholesale allocation is explained by contrast with the warehouse's allocation of a unit to an order, which the moment of promise introduces. The service needs all three (numbers, moments, channels), since its component table says which system writes which number and its requirements table says which interaction must be exact. The choices come after the service because the service is one of the four and the other three are judged against it; the trade-offs come before the stages because the stage table uses the criteria the trade-offs name (lag, writers, buffers) as its warning signs. Kestrel & Pine's W1 is named in the scene and shown in the service section before the choices; the reader knows it from Part I as a decision already taken, and the choices then say what it was chosen over. The worked example comes after the choices and the stages because it applies the chosen option (W1) to the opening case at the Omnichannel stage; before the choices it would be a list of remedies with no names. The failures come last because every design must expect them, the recommended one included, and the section ends on the count's own accuracy, the one failure a reconciliation cannot find; the reconciliation and the buffer are what the conclusion and the part closing start from. Moving the scene later would put four sections of vocabulary before the problem; moving the failures before the choices would describe faults of a design the reader has not met.

hook.content: A web shopper and a store customer try to buy the last jacket within the same minute. Both channels show it as available, but there is only one unit on the shelf.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone has seen 'in stock' on a product page, and the search results of the previous chapter have just shown Eva that label.
bridge.to_topic: A shelf count cannot produce that label: some units belong to unshipped orders and others are held back, so the label is a calculation, and the question is who makes it and how every channel gets the same answer.

thesis_statement.text: Availability is computed from the count, the claims against it and the units held back, in one place, before a channel commits to a sale; copying a stock number along a chain of scheduled updates leaves channels selling from different answers.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout (all three bullets) and paragraph p02

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and paragraph p03

promises.promise: Start from Kestrel & Pine's worst evening of 2026, the Black Friday Oversell.
Take 'in stock' apart into the numbers behind it, and say when a unit becomes promised.

Add several locations and channels, and describe the availability service: which system writes which number, what each step of a purchase needs, and why stock changes should travel as events and not as scheduled copies.
Compare four ways of computing availability, weigh their trade-offs and say which fits which scale stage.
Work the Oversell through with the remedy in place, list the ways stock integrations fail, and check the count itself against a study of inventory records.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A web shopper and a store customer who try to buy the last jacket in the same minute can both succeed if each channel relies on its own stock count, so the channels need a shared way to decide which sale gets the unit.

evidence.what: Two channels, one unit on the shelf, two sales within a minute.
evidence.shows: The chapter's problem in one case: two answers to one question about one unit.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A shelf count alone cannot say whether a unit may be sold, because some units already belong to orders and others are held back, so availability has to combine those facts before a channel commits to a sale, and copying a number along scheduled updates leaves channels with different answers.

transition_in.carries_over: The need for a shared way to decide which sale gets the last unit.
transition_in.introduces: Why a count is not that answer: the claims and holds a count leaves out, and the chapter's claim that availability is a calculation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In Eva's order the search results have just shown the Ridgewalker 'in stock', and availability is what supplies that label, the cart's stock check and the commitment at checkout that keeps another shopper from buying her unit.

transition_in.carries_over: Availability as a calculation made before a channel commits to a sale.
transition_in.introduces: Where that calculation is used in Eva's order, starting from the 'in stock' label the previous chapter's search results showed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter starts from Kestrel & Pine's Black Friday Oversell, takes 'in stock' apart into its numbers, says when a unit becomes promised, adds locations and channels, describes the availability service, compares four ways of computing availability with their trade-offs and by scale stage, works the Oversell through with the remedy in place and ends with the ways stock integrations fail and the accuracy of the count itself; its evidence is the Oversell, vendors' platform documentation and a study of inventory records.

transition_in.carries_over: The three places in Eva's order where availability is used.
transition_in.introduces: The order in which the chapter explains how that answer is computed, and its evidence: the Oversell, platform documentation and a study of inventory records.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: Friday 27 November 2026, 19:40
sections.controlling_idea: On Black Friday 2026 Kestrel & Pine oversold 1,340 jackets while every system was up, because stock counts were copied along a chain of scheduled updates and nobody had decided who owned the number.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case the chapter explains: an oversell caused by scheduled copying and several writers, with no system down.

flow.rationale: The chain as it was built, the lag it produced, the evening minute by minute, what made it worse, then the CEO's question: the reader needs the chain before the timeline can be read, and the question only after seeing that nothing was broken.

transition_in.carries_over: The claim that copying a stock number along scheduled updates leaves channels selling from different answers.
transition_in.introduces: The evening on which that happened at Kestrel & Pine.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In January 2027 Noor Visser asked Ruben Alves and Daniel Okafor to reconstruct the Black Friday Oversell minute by minute, and what they drew was a chain.

In 2026 the warehouse management system sent counts to the ERP every 15 minutes, the ERP (which also keeps what the stock is worth in the books) copied them to the shop platform hourly, and the platform copied them hourly to the marketplace connector.

evidence.what: WMS to ERP every 15 minutes, ERP to shop platform hourly, shop platform to marketplace connector hourly.
evidence.shows: Stock reached each channel as a copy of a copy, each on its own clock.

transition_in.carries_over: The chain on the whiteboard.
transition_in.introduces: Its three hops and the schedule of each.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A sale on one channel therefore reached the other channels only after picking and the scheduled updates, up to two hours later.

evidence.what: Up to two hours for a sale to reduce the stock shown elsewhere.
evidence.shows: The lag is a property of the chain, not a fault in it.

transition_in.carries_over: The three scheduled hops.
transition_in.introduces: The lag they add up to for a sale on one channel.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On Friday 27 November the Ridgewalker sold out in the warehouse at 19:40 and the channels went on selling it, the marketplaces until after 21:05; the timeline shows how long each channel went on selling, and 1,340 units were oversold on 1,120 orders, about 790 of the units sold on the storefronts and 550 on the marketplaces.

evidence.what: Timeline of 27 November 2026: 19:40 last units picked; 19:45 the WMS tells the ERP; 20:00-21:00 peak hour of 2,300 orders, 38 a minute; about 20:30 the ERP tells the platform (illustrative time); 21:05 the Ridgewalker set to zero by hand in the connector; Saturday 1,340 units oversold, 1,120 orders affected.
evidence.shows: Each row shows which systems still believed the jacket was in stock, so the reader sees the news of the empty shelf arrive one hop at a time.

evidence.what: Of the 1,340 oversold units about 790 were storefront orders and 550 marketplace orders (illustrative split); the marketplace share carried the penalties.
evidence.shows: Both kinds of channel oversold, and the marketplace share cost most.

evidence.what: Figure 1: the Oversell as a relay.
evidence.shows: Each hand-off waited for its schedule while carts kept arriving.

transition_in.carries_over: The chain and its lag of up to two hours.
transition_in.introduces: The evening the lag met a peak hour, as a timeline.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two things made it worse: the order queue to the warehouse backed up for four hours, and three of the shop platform's 41 apps could write inventory, one of which had already caused two weeks of phantom reservations in March 2026.

evidence.what: Four-hour backlog of the order queue to the WMS; the App That Wrote Stock, March 2026, about 600 variants for two weeks.
evidence.shows: Lag was not the only cause: the count itself arrived late, and the number had more than one writer.

transition_in.carries_over: The timeline of the evening.
transition_in.introduces: Two aggravating facts: a queue backlog and apps that wrote the same number as the warehouse feed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The CEO asked why the website did not know, and Noor's answer, which became Waypoint decision W1, was that it could not know because nobody had decided who owned the number and nothing carried changes fast enough.

transition_in.carries_over: The lag and the several writers.
transition_in.introduces: The question they raise and the answer the rest of the chapter gives in full.

sections.heading: What "In Stock" Means: Five Numbers, Not One
sections.controlling_idea: 'In stock' is not one number: on hand is a counted fact, committed, reserved and held-back units are claims against it, and what a channel may sell is derived from them.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the numbers and the derivation the thesis names, and shows four vendors separating them in the same way.

flow.rationale: The five numbers, then the formula that needs them, then the vendors' names for the same things, then one vendor stating the arithmetic and changing a state's meaning, then who owns which number: the ownership rule needs the reader to know which numbers are counted and which are derived.

transition_in.carries_over: 'Nobody had decided who owned the number.'
transition_in.introduces: That the number is five numbers and a calculation, which is why ownership had not been decided.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every system that tracks stock separates the units physically present from the units it may still promise, using five numbers: on hand, committed, reserved, held back and incoming.
The number a channel may sell, available-to-promise, is derived: on hand minus committed, minus reserved, minus held back, plus incoming only if the merchant promises against it.

evidence.what: available-to-promise = on hand − committed − reserved − held back (+ incoming, only if you promise against it), stated as industry practice.
evidence.shows: The reader can compute what a channel may sell from the other numbers.

evidence.what: Figure 2: on hand as the one counted fact, the claims against it and what remains.
evidence.shows: Available is a remainder, not a count.

transition_in.carries_over: The five numbers.
transition_in.introduces: The figure derived from them and its formula.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopify, commercetools, Adobe Commerce and SAP Commerce all separate physical units, units promised to orders and units sellable now, under different names; three of them say 'reserved' for what this chapter calls committed.

evidence.what: The author's alignment of four vendors' terms for physical units, promised units, sellable units, deliberate holds and location.
evidence.shows: The separation is common to the vendors, so it is not one platform's idea; the alignment is the author's.
evidence.source: Vendor documentation, dated in the table

transition_in.carries_over: The formula as industry practice.
transition_in.introduces: Four vendors' vocabularies aligned to it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopify's documentation states the arithmetic outright: on hand is the sum of the available, committed, reserved and held-back states, and incoming is not part of it.

evidence.what: On hand "equals the sum of inventory quantities that are in the available, committed, reserved, damaged, safety_stock, and quality_control states"; POS gained 'On hand' and 'Unavailable' states on 9 February 2023.
evidence.shows: A vendor publishes the same arithmetic the formula gives.
evidence.source: Shopify developer documentation, n.d., accessed November 2026; Shopify changelog, 2023-02-09

transition_in.carries_over: The four vendors' vocabularies.
transition_in.introduces: One vendor's own statement of the sum.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On 5 August 2026 Shopify moved some holds from reserved to committed, so an integration that subtracted reserved in its own calculation changed behavior without a code change: the meaning of a stock state can move under the systems that read it.

evidence.what: Draft-order and transfer holds moved from `reserved` to `committed`; `available` and `on_hand` unchanged.
evidence.shows: A system that recomputes available from another system's states depends on definitions it does not control.

transition_in.carries_over: Shopify's states and their sum.
transition_in.introduces: A dated change to what one state means.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each number has an owner except the derived one: the warehouse owns on hand, the order-taking system owns committed, and nobody should own 'available', because it is a computation; most oversells begin when a system stores it as a fact and lets another overwrite it.

transition_in.carries_over: The numbers, the formula and the vendors' practice.
transition_in.introduces: Who owns which number, and why the derived one has no owner.

sections.heading: When a Unit Becomes Promised: Reservations and Allocations
sections.controlling_idea: A unit can leave the available number at add-to-cart, at order creation or at fulfillment; the choice is a business one with a cost on each side, and each leaves a window in which two buyers can get the same unit.

advances_thesis.how: Sets out the three moments and their costs, and shows that even the common default leaves a window of seconds.

flow.rationale: The claim that the moment is a choice, the vendors' configuration as evidence, the three moments compared, then what the published window means at peak: the comparison table needs the vendors' modes, and the window is the cost of the row most merchants choose.

transition_in.carries_over: Committed and reserved as claims against on hand.
transition_in.introduces: The moment at which a claim is made, which the definitions left open.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The platforms disagree about when a unit leaves the available number (in the cart, at order creation or at the warehouse's allocation), and expose the choice as configuration because it is a business choice with a cost on each side.

Three vendors show the range: commercetools offers three inventory modes per cart and publishes a delay of up to 10 seconds, Adobe Commerce reserves when an order is submitted, and Shopify commits at order creation; a vendor's 'reserve' at order creation is what this chapter calls committing.

evidence.what: commercetools: TrackOnly, ReserveOnOrder, ReserveOnCart (expiry 1 to 44,640 minutes), eventual consistency of up to 10 seconds; Adobe Commerce: reservation at order submission, compensating reservation on cancellation; Shopify: committed at order creation and while on hold.
evidence.shows: The three moments are real product settings, not a theoretical classification.
evidence.source: commercetools API documentation, n.d., accessed November 2026; Adobe Commerce documentation, updated 2026-08-20; Shopify Help Center, n.d.

transition_in.carries_over: The choice exposed as configuration.
transition_in.introduces: Three vendors' documented settings.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each of the three moments protects something different and costs something different: the cart protects the shopper and ties up stock, order creation uses stock best and leaves a window of seconds, and allocation at fulfillment keeps the warehouse flexible and accepts orders it may not fill.

evidence.what: Three moments (add to cart, order creation, allocation at fulfillment) against protects, costs and fits.
evidence.shows: The reader can pick a moment from the kind of sale: scarce-stock drops, ordinary selling, wholesale and backorders.

evidence.what: Figure 3: a unit's life from available through reserved or committed to shipped.
evidence.shows: The states a unit passes through and the two ways it returns to available.

transition_in.carries_over: The vendors' settings.
transition_in.introduces: The three moments side by side: what each protects, what it costs and where it fits.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A window of 10 seconds is six orders at Kestrel & Pine's peak rate, enough to oversell a hot item; every platform has such a window and most do not publish it.

evidence.what: 38 orders a minute for 10 seconds is about six orders.
evidence.shows: A published, small window is still large enough to matter on a peak day.

transition_in.carries_over: The 'window of seconds' in the order-creation row.
transition_in.introduces: What that window is worth at 38 orders a minute.

sections.heading: Many Locations, Many Channels
sections.controlling_idea: With stock in several places and promises made in several channels, one physical pool is promised many times, so availability is published per channel with a buffer, and sourcing, allocations and promises against incoming stock become separate decisions.

advances_thesis.how: Shows why, with more than one location and channel, one figure per channel has to be derived from a shared pool, which is the case for computing it in one place.

additional_patterns.applies_to: the three rules (buffer per channel, sourcing, allocations)

flow.rationale: Kestrel & Pine's several stock places first, then the two definitions (location, channel) the rules are stated in, then the three rules, then the two cases that promise stock not on hand: the rules cannot be read before 'per channel' and 'location' mean something.

transition_in.carries_over: Everything so far: one shelf and one shop.
transition_in.introduces: Several shelves and several shops, as at Kestrel & Pine.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine has neither one shelf nor one shop: its stock sits at Duiven, in six stores and in a marketplace's fulfillment program warehouse.

evidence.what: Duiven; six stores of about 1,800 variants each; a marketplace fulfillment program warehouse in Germany holding about 40% of the units sold on that marketplace there.
evidence.shows: The single-shelf assumption fails for an ordinary mid-size brand.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A location is any place from which stock can be promised and shipped, each with its own count and its own counting system; a marketplace's warehouse is the hardest case because the merchant sees its count and cannot check it.

transition_in.carries_over: The places where Kestrel & Pine's stock sits.
transition_in.introduces: The term for such a place, and the one the merchant cannot count.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A channel is a place where a promise is made, availability is published per channel, and one physical pool may be promised to several channels at once; three consequences follow.

transition_in.carries_over: Where stock sits.
transition_in.introduces: Where it is promised, and that one pool serves several such places.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each channel gets its own buffer, largest where an oversell costs most, and because a buffer withholds sellable units it is a business setting.

evidence.what: A marketplace oversell brings a seller-performance penalty and, repeated, a suspended listing.
evidence.shows: The cost of an oversell differs by channel, so the buffer should too.

evidence.what: Figure 4: one pool, many promises, with a buffer layer.
evidence.shows: Every channel draws on the same stock; the buffer is what no channel may sell.

transition_in.carries_over: One pool promised to several channels.
transition_in.introduces: The first rule: availability per channel, with a buffer per channel.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Which location fulfills a line is a separate decision from whether the unit is available, and once it needs capacity, cut-off times or carrier cost it belongs to an order management system.

evidence.what: Adobe Commerce's source priority and distance priority algorithms; Shopify's fulfillment order.
evidence.shows: Platforms ship simple sourcing; anything richer is the order management system's.
evidence.source: Adobe Commerce documentation, updated 2026-08-20; Shopify developer docs, n.d.

transition_in.carries_over: The first rule, about channels.
transition_in.introduces: The second rule, about locations: sourcing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Wholesale needs allocations in a second sense of the word: earlier 'allocated' and 'allocation at fulfillment' meant assigning a unit to a placed order, whereas a wholesale allocation sets part of the pool aside in advance for a customer, a season or a channel, which none of the four platforms holds per customer.

evidence.what: A wholesale buyer who ordered 240 jackets for spring should not compete with Friday-evening shoppers.
evidence.shows: Without an allocation the storefront can sell units a wholesale order is counting on.

transition_in.carries_over: The first two rules.
transition_in.introduces: The third rule: an advance claim on the pool for a wholesale customer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A backorder and a pre-order promise stock that is not on hand, which is legitimate only if the incoming quantity is tracked and the date is honest.

evidence.what: Directive 2011/83/EU, Article 18: delivery within 30 days unless agreed otherwise.
evidence.shows: An open-ended backorder is a legal risk as well as a service one.

transition_in.carries_over: The three consequences, all about stock that is on hand.
transition_in.introduces: Two cases that promise stock that is not.

sections.heading: How the Pieces Fit: The Availability Service
sections.controlling_idea: The arrangement that keeps one answer per channel separates counting, order-taking and deriving, gives each number one writer, asks for an exact answer only at checkout, and carries stock changes as events instead of scheduled snapshots.

advances_thesis.how: Describes the one place that computes the figure, the single writer of each number, the exact commit at checkout and the event in place of the scheduled copy.

flow.rationale: The components and their writers, then Kestrel & Pine's W1 as that arrangement, then what each interaction needs from it, then the one interaction that must be exact, then how changes should reach it and public examples of both ways: the requirements per interaction presuppose the service, and the event-against-sync comparison presupposes knowing which interactions tolerate lag.

transition_in.carries_over: One pool, several locations and channels, buffers and allocations: several things to combine for every channel.
transition_in.introduces: The arrangement that combines them in one place.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With several locations and channels, counting stock, taking orders and deriving availability are three responsibilities with one writer per number, connected by stock events, and a reconciliation job compares the service's copies with the systems that count and commit, on a schedule.

evidence.what: Four components (stock-counting systems, order-taking systems, the availability service, the reconciliation job) with what each is responsible for, writes and never writes.
evidence.shows: Every number has exactly one writer, and 'available' is written only by the service that derives it.

evidence.what: Figure 5: the Waypoint target.
evidence.shows: Counts and commitments flow in, available per channel flows out, and reconciliation checks the copies against the counts.

sections.heading: The Choices
sections.controlling_idea: A growing merchant has four ways to compute availability (the platform's own stock, a stock master with periodic sync, an event-driven availability service, a fulfillment provider's shared pool), and each is right for a stage and a limit at the next.

advances_thesis.how: Places 'computed by the shop platform' and 'computed by one service' among the realistic options and says when each holds.

flow.rationale: The four options in the order a growing merchant meets them, which is also Kestrel & Pine's own history; the provider's pool comes last because it hands the problem to someone else.

transition_in.carries_over: The availability service as the clean arrangement.
transition_in.introduces: That it is one of four options, and not the right one for every merchant.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: There are four realistic ways to compute availability, each right for a stage and a limit at the next.
The platform's own stock fields work while there is one location and the platform is the only system that takes orders.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine in 2016-2018 with its Tiel 3PL.
evidence.shows: The simplest option was right for the company's first stage.

transition_in.carries_over: Four ways.
transition_in.introduces: The first, where most merchants start.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An ERP or WMS as stock master with periodic sync is the common arrangement at the Growing stage, and its limit is structural: the copy is a snapshot, the schedule is a lag, and each hop adds its own clock.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's January 2027 landscape; the Oversell is what it does at peak.
evidence.shows: The option fails at peak for a reason built into it.

transition_in.carries_over: The platform's own stock.
transition_in.introduces: The second option, which Kestrel & Pine ran in January 2027.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An event-driven availability service, bought or built, costs integration work on every counting and ordering system and the discipline of one writer per state.

transition_in.carries_over: The stock master with periodic sync.
transition_in.introduces: The third option, W1, and what it costs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A fulfillment provider's shared pool moves the availability problem to the provider, at the price of the merchant's control over the count and the buffer.

evidence.what: Zalando's ZEOS and NEXT, November 2024: "a unified stock pool and an advanced order management system"; 24 markets and 18 sales channels by March 2026.
evidence.shows: A provider's pool across channels is an offered product.

transition_in.carries_over: The availability service a merchant runs.
transition_in.introduces: The fourth option, where someone else runs it.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.controlling_idea: The four options differ in lag, in the number of writers of 'available', in buffers and allocations, in integration cost and in how they break; keep platform stock until a second system takes orders or counts stock, name the owners before building a connector, and consider a separate service when two of four conditions hold.

advances_thesis.how: States the condition under which the platform stops being the one place, and why owners are named before a connector is built.

transition_in.carries_over: The four options one by one.
transition_in.introduces: The same four compared on the criteria that decide between them, then the author's recommendation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The four options compare on five things: how long other channels take to learn of a sale, how many systems write 'available', whether buffers and allocations are possible, what integration costs and how each option breaks.

evidence.what: Four options against lag, number of writers of 'available', per-channel buffers and wholesale allocations, integration cost and when it breaks.
evidence.shows: Only the availability service has seconds of lag, one writer and buffers under the merchant's control; the sync chain has the most lag and the most writers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The comparison favors the availability service on lag, writers and buffers, yet the author would keep platform stock until another system starts taking orders or counting stock, and then assign owners for physical and committed stock before building the connector, because a connector without that agreement copies two incompatible answers.

transition_in.carries_over: The comparison.
transition_in.introduces: What the author would do, and in which order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A separate availability service is worth considering when any two of four conditions apply (multiple locations, multiple order channels, location-specific promises, wholesale allocations); Kestrel & Pine met that test in 2023 and built the copying chain instead.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine met the test in 2023; W1 replaces the chain.
evidence.shows: The test would have told the company three years before the Oversell.

transition_in.carries_over: When to leave platform stock.
transition_in.introduces: When to go further, to a separate service, and when a provider's pool suits.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: What is typical, what becomes necessary and what warns that an approach is outgrown change at each of the four scale stages, while three things do not change: one system counts on hand per location, available is derived, and the last unit at checkout is committed atomically.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the shop platform as the one place at the Starting stage and the service at the Omnichannel stage, with the same three rules at both.

transition_in.carries_over: 'Each is right for a stage' and the conditions for moving on.
transition_in.introduces: The same advice laid out stage by stage, with warning signs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stock handling changes with scale more than most topics because stock is the fact most systems copy, but at every stage on hand is counted by one system per location, available is derived, and the last unit at checkout is committed atomically.

evidence.what: Four stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group) against what is typical, what becomes necessary and the warning signs, with Kestrel & Pine's years.
evidence.shows: The reader can find their own stage and read off the next step and the signs that it is due; a Starting merchant gets the three constants from the platform, an Omnichannel merchant must arrange them.

sections.heading: In Practice
sections.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's reconstruction finds three causes of the Oversell (lag by design, several writers, no buffer and no reconciliation), each of which W1 answers without bringing oversells to zero.

advances_thesis.how: Works the thesis's remedy through the opening case cause by cause, and shows that a buffer and a reconciliation remain necessary.

additional_patterns.applies_to: the three causes, each with its remedy

flow.rationale: The three causes, each with W1's answer, then the evening replayed with W1 in place. The replay needs all three remedies, and its last sentence (not zero) is what the next section starts from.

transition_in.carries_over: The Omnichannel stage, where a merchant must arrange deliberately what a Starting merchant gets from the platform.
transition_in.introduces: Kestrel & Pine as the merchant at that stage that had not, and the Oversell worked through cause by cause.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine is the Omnichannel merchant that had not arranged these things: seen from later in 2027, the reconstruction of the opening scene shows three causes of the Oversell, and W1 answers each.
The first cause was lag by design: three hops on their own clocks, up to two hours end to end, which W1 replaces with stock events from the WMS to the availability service.

evidence.what: 38 orders a minute makes one hour of blindness 2,300 orders.
evidence.shows: The lag's size in orders.

transition_in.carries_over: Three causes.
transition_in.introduces: The first, and W1's answer to it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The second cause was several writers: six could change Duiven stock, four of them automated flows into the shop platform, so the platform's number could change in four ways without anyone deciding it; W1 names one writer per state.

evidence.what: Six writers: the WMS feed (through the ERP's hourly sync), hand adjustments in the ERP, hand edits in the platform admin, three apps; four automated flows into the platform: the hourly sync and the three apps.
evidence.shows: The number had no single owner, so any correction could be undone by another writer.

transition_in.carries_over: The first cause.
transition_in.introduces: The second, and W1's answer to it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The third cause was no buffer and no reconciliation: every channel sold to the last unit and nothing compared the WMS with the platform, so the copies drifted unseen, as the first weekly reconciliation, begun in May 2027, later showed; W1 adds a per-channel buffer and a weekly reconciliation.

evidence.what: First weekly reconciliation, May 2027: 2.3% of active variants with a different quantity; buffers of 3 units per SKU for marketplaces and 1 for the storefronts (illustrative); reconciliation weekly, daily in November.
evidence.shows: Differences existed unseen for months, and the buffer is a number someone now chooses.

transition_in.carries_over: The second cause.
transition_in.introduces: The third, and W1's answer to it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Had W1 existed on 27 November 2026, the oversell would have shrunk from 1,340 units to the few that pass through the marketplace's own push interval: no availability design reaches zero, and the goal is a window seconds wide and a deliberate buffer.

transition_in.carries_over: The three causes and their remedies.
transition_in.introduces: The evening replayed with all three remedies in place, and what remains.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Stock integrations fail in a small number of recurring ways, each with a detection and a recovery; the reconciliation job detects most of them, so an integration without one is not finished, and the one failure it cannot detect, a wrong count, needs controls of its own.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that events and single writers still fail in known ways and that a scheduled comparison of copy with source is what finds the failures.

transition_in.carries_over: 'No availability design reaches zero oversells.'
transition_in.introduces: The ways in which even the event-driven design fails, and how each is found and repaired.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Seven failures recur in stock integrations (duplicated events, out-of-order events, snapshot overwrite, two writers, a counting system outage, identifier mismatch, a wrong count), and each has a detection and a recovery.

evidence.what: Seven failures against what each looks like, how it is detected and how it is recovered.
evidence.shows: Each failure is recognizable from its symptom and has a known repair; the Kestrel & Pine incidents appear as rows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two failures are detected by a variance between a copy and its source, which is what the reconciliation job finds; a stock integration without one is not finished, because every delivery mechanism delivers at least once and sometimes not at all.

evidence.what: Delivery "isn't always guaranteed"; "use reconciliation jobs to periodically fetch data". Waypoint W5 makes a reconciliation job a condition of every integration.
evidence.shows: The vendor that sends the events tells receivers not to rely on them alone.
evidence.source: Shopify webhook documentation, n.d., accessed November 2026

transition_in.carries_over: The detection column of the table, where a variance recurs.
transition_in.introduces: The one control most of the failures share, and the vendor instruction and Waypoint decision that require it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A reconciliation compares every copy with the count and cannot tell whether the count itself is right, and published research finds it often is not: a 2008 study of one US retailer found 65% of nearly 370,000 inventory records inaccurate, and later reviews report 20% to 67%.

evidence.what: 65% of nearly 370,000 records inaccurate across 37 stores of one US retailer; 20% to 67% across later studies.
evidence.shows: Record inaccuracy is common enough that no synchronization design can assume a correct count; an old, pre-RFID study of one retailer, not a current industry rate.
evidence.source: DeHoratius and Raman, Management Science, April 2008; Production journal review, 2018

transition_in.carries_over: The reconciliation job, which compares copies with the systems that count.
transition_in.introduces: The one failure in the table it cannot find: a wrong count, and how common that is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Count accuracy therefore needs its own controls beside the integration: cycle counting, which checks part of the physical stock on a rolling schedule, and safety buffers for the uncertainty that remains.

transition_in.carries_over: How often the counted fact is wrong.
transition_in.introduces: The two controls that answer it: cycle counting and a buffer.

flow.rationale: All seven failures, then the control most of them share, then the one failure that control cannot find, with the research that measures it and the two controls that answer it: the count-accuracy paragraphs need the table's last row and the reconciliation job before them, and read earlier (they once opened 'In Practice') they were a topic the section then left.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The five numbers, the moment of promise, the per-channel figure and the failures are one answer seen from four sides: there is one counted fact per location and everything else is a claim on it or a calculation from it, so the only decisions are who writes each number, how fast a change travels and what compares the copies. For the part: the season typed four times, the Price Drift, the Stacking Bug, the jacket nobody could find and the Oversell are one problem, a value shown or used by a system that did not own it with nothing comparing it to the system that did, and each chapter's remedy has the same three parts.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant can write the ownership of each stock number down before any product is bought, and the same list (owner, who may write, how each channel learns of a change, what compares the copy with the source) can be made for product content, price and discount; none of Kestrel & Pine's 2027 remedies replaces the shop platform.

takeaway.content: Write down who owns each stock number before the first connector is built, size the buffer per channel from measurement, and take the eight questions to your own company; then, for product content, price, discount and stock, write down the owner, who may write, how each channel learns of a change and what compares the copy with the source, starting with stock.
